article.title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
article.subtitle: Can Democrats still win the Senate if the polls overestimate them? And how ugly could the map get for Republicans if the polls are wrong in the other…

extraction.summary: Model Talk stress-testing FLIPR's Senate forecast against systematic polling error. First it applies uniform 2, 3 and 4-point shifts to the polling averages. Then it splits the day's 40,000 FLIPR Deluxe simulations into thirds by the uniform national error draw, which comes from a Student's t distribution: modest error, error against Democrats averaging 3.5 points, and error against Republicans averaging 3.5 points. Democrats win the Senate in 87.8, 37.7 and 99.3 percent of those buckets. The piece confirms what else FLIPR simulates (state, regional, demographic and race-level errors), that probabilities reflect blended-forecast error rather than poll error, and how ranked-choice voting in Alaska affects Peltola.

findings.statement: In each of FLIPR's 40,000 daily simulations, the uniform national forecast error is drawn from a Student's t distribution, and additional random draws simulate correlated errors (e.g. systematic error among Hispanics) and uncorrelated local errors (e.g. one congressional district).
findings.evidence_quote: In each sim, FLIPR draws a random number from a Student’s t distribution to simulate uniform, national polling error.

findings.statement: Silver Bulletin defines a 'normal-sized polling error' as 3 to 4 points in the same direction across states, about the margin by which polls underestimated Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Larger systematic errors are in the tails.
findings.evidence_quote: I’m choosing 3-4 points since that’s basically what we refer to as a “normal-sized polling error” around these parts.

findings.statement: Splitting FLIPR Deluxe simulations into thirds by the national error draw: when the error is modest (within about 1.3 points), Democrats win the House 100 percent (238 seats) and the Senate 87.8 percent (52.4 seats). With an error against Democrats (R+1.4 or worse, averaging 3.5): House 81.4 percent (224), Senate 37.7 percent (49.7). With an error against Republicans (averaging 3.5): House 100 percent (254), Senate 99.3 percent (54.6).

quantities.name: Senate D prob, error vs D
Senate D prob, error vs R

findings.evidence_quote: On average in this scenario, the forecast overestimates Democrats by 3.5 points

findings.statement: FLIPR's probabilities reflect the estimated error of its blended forecasts (polls plus fundamentals, plus expert ratings in Deluxe), not just the error of the polling averages; Silver notes that 'polling errors' in this context are technically forecast errors.
findings.evidence_quote: The probabilities you see in FLIPR are based on the errors it estimates in these blended forecasts and not just the error associated with the polling averages on their own.

findings.statement: FLIPR simulates regional and demographic polling errors without privileging any one, considering Midwestern underperformance by Democrats, as in 2016, alongside Southern underperformance, Hispanic overperformance, Midwestern overperformance and others. Even with national error held near zero, Senate win probabilities stay uncertain, for example Texas only rising from 71.5 to 76.0 percent for Talarico.

quantities.name: Talarico win prob default vs modest-error

findings.rationale: Congressional races are correlated but less than presidential ones.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR does consider exactly this scenario, although it doesn’t privilege it.

findings.statement: In Alaska, FLIPR explicitly plays out ranked-choice reallocations, so minor Republicans' votes mostly transfer to incumbent Dan Sullivan, making FLIPR more bearish on Peltola than models that look at first-round margins.
findings.evidence_quote: I think this is because it’s explicitly playing out the RCV process when other models might not be.

findings.statement: When polling averages are thin, as in South Dakota, the advanced FLIPR versions heavily hedge toward fundamentals rather than taking polls at face value.
findings.evidence_quote: The more advanced versions of FLIPR heavily hedge toward the “fundamentals” in these cases

findings.statement: Uniform-shift stress tests on Senate polling averages: as-is, Democrats 54-46; polls overrating Democrats by 2 points, 52-48 Democratic; by 3 points, a 50-50 tie; by 4 points, Republicans 52-48. Many narrow leads, as in the 2012 and 2016 presidential maps, make the outcome sensitive to small systematic errors.
findings.evidence_quote: With a 3-point polling error, though, Maine and Texas turn into narrow GOP wins, and Democrats would top out at 50 seats.

findings.statement: Republicans would need roughly a 5-point uniform error to make the House a toss-up in October 2026. Competitive House races are spread evenly across the map, so regional misses tend to offset when overall polls are right.

quantities.name: uniform error needed for House toss-up

findings.evidence_quote: Republicans would need something like a 5-point uniform polling error to turn the House back into a toss-up

findings.statement: Predicting polling error means predicting the behavior of pollsters, who are aware of past errors and adjust their methods.
findings.evidence_quote: So in predicting polling error, in some sense you’re predicting the behavior of human beings and how they adjust to changing conditions in the polling landscape.

findings.statement: FLIPR counts certain independents toward Democratic control, such as Seth Bodnar in Montana.
findings.evidence_quote: More likely in the form of independent Seth Bodnar — whom FLIPR counts toward Democratic control

political_insights.insight: Many Republicans in red states and districts had not faced a strong Democratic year since 2018, for example Roger Marshall in Kansas.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Incumbent strength measured in neutral years may overstate resilience in wave years.

political_insights.insight: Unusually, reported Republican internal polling in October 2026 was nearly as bad for Republicans as public polling.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Leaked internals agreeing with public polls reduces the chance of a hidden bias.

open_questions: Degrees of freedom and scale of the Student's t distribution used for national error.
